hook_text: Play a song at triple speed. Does it get louder? No — and that one fact is the most-tested trap in trig graphs.
clip_script: Here's the trap that catches thousands of learners every year. The graph of sine three x — what does the three do? Most people's instinct: it's multiplying, so the wave must get taller. Wrong — and music already taught you why. Sine of three x is a song played at triple speed. Every note arrives in a third of the time, so a full verse that used to need three hundred and sixty degrees now squeezes into one twenty — three complete waves where one used to live. But play any song at triple speed and ask: is it louder? Of course not. Faster is not louder. The three is inside the bracket, so it spends the angle faster — but sine's answer still lives between one and minus one, so the peaks never move. Height untouched. Want louder? That's a different knob: three sine x, with the three outside, catching the answer and tripling it — peaks at three, period still three sixty. Inside changes speed. Outside changes volume. Two dials, zero crosstalk. So when a sketch shows three little waves crammed into the window, read it calmly: cycles give you k equals three, peaks give you the amplitude, and never let one dial impersonate the other. That's the exact misunderstanding the examiners fish for — and you just became uncatchable.
visual_style: A music player UI over a sine wave; hitting 3x speed squeezes three waves into the window while a volume meter stays pinned at the same level; then the volume knob turns and the wave grows tall while the speed stays put — two dials side by side, glowing independently.
mood: Snappy and confident — a gotcha defused with a picture everyone already owns.
pacing: Fast hook question, beat of suspense, crisp inside-versus-outside reveal, rapid two-dial recap.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and master all four knobs.
